title: Carillion: The Company That Ran Britain, Then Collapsed

beats.say: If you lived in Britain in twenty seventeen, there's a good chance Carillion touched your life. It built hospitals and roads, maintained prisons and army bases, and served school meals. Then, in January twenty eighteen, it collapsed almost overnight.

vis.text: It ran half of Britain. Then it vanished.

beats.say: When it went into liquidation, Carillion had liabilities of almost seven billion pounds. It was one of the biggest corporate collapses in modern British history.

Around forty three thousand people worked for it worldwide, including nearly twenty thousand in Britain. Thousands of small firms were waiting to be paid. And taxpayers were left with part of the bill.
Part one. The giant.

Carillion was formed in nineteen ninety nine, spun out of the building firm Tarmac. It grew by winning huge contracts, many of them from the government. Schools, hospitals, railways, defence sites, even the new high speed railway, HS2.
It was what's called a strategic supplier to the government. In other words, so big and so involved in public services that people assumed it couldn't be allowed to fail.

vis.text: Too big to fail. Or so people assumed.

beats.say: Even after warning signs appeared, the government kept awarding Carillion big contracts, including part of HS2. That decision was heavily criticised after the collapse.

vis.text: Contracts kept coming, even after warnings.

beats.say: Part two. Winning at any price.
The problem started with how Carillion won its work. To beat rivals, it often bid low. Very low. Sometimes so low that the contracts would only make money if absolutely everything went perfectly.
And in construction, things rarely go perfectly. Projects run late. Costs rise. Surprises appear when you dig into the ground. Every problem ate into thin profits.

vis.text: In construction, things rarely go perfectly.

beats.say: Two giant hospital projects became disasters. The Royal Liverpool University Hospital and the Midland Metropolitan Hospital near Birmingham ran badly late, with serious construction problems, and costs spiralling.
The Royal Liverpool hospital was eventually finished years late, by other builders, at extra public cost. Patients and staff waited far longer than planned for their new hospital.

vis.text: Years late, at extra public cost.

beats.say: Part three. Counting money early.
Carillion's accounts were optimistic. It often recognised revenue on contracts based on what it expected to earn, including payments it hoped to win from customers, before the money arrived.
On paper, it looked healthy. But cash was a different story. And for a business, cash is what pays the wages and the bills.

vis.text: On paper, healthy. In cash, not.

beats.say: Carillion also bought other companies, and recorded large amounts of goodwill on its books. Goodwill is the extra value you claim a business has, beyond its physical assets. If that value isn't real, the company is weaker than it looks.
Part four. Squeezing the small firms.

To keep cash flowing, Carillion leaned on its suppliers. It could take up to a hundred and twenty days to pay small businesses for work they'd already done. Effectively, small firms were lending money to a giant.
When Carillion collapsed, around thirty thousand suppliers and subcontractors were owed roughly a billion pounds. For many small firms, that was devastating.
Some small businesses had to lay off staff or close altogether. They'd done the work, in good faith, and never got paid.

vis.text: They did the work, and never got paid.

beats.say: Part five. Dividends and debt.

Meanwhile, Carillion kept rewarding shareholders. A later parliamentary report found it raised its dividend every year, regardless of how the business was really doing. Debt kept growing. And the pension scheme had a large deficit.
The report said the board seemed more focused on protecting dividends and bonuses than on the long term health of the company and its pension scheme.
Part six. The collapse.

In July twenty seventeen, Carillion issued a profit warning, announcing an eight hundred and forty five million pound write down on its contracts. Its shares crashed. More warnings followed. Talks with banks and the government failed.
On the fifteenth of January twenty eighteen, Carillion went into compulsory liquidation. Because it ran so many public services, the government had to step in to keep them going.

Hospital construction stopped. Prisons, schools and military contracts had to be taken over or moved to other firms. The cost to taxpayers of handling the collapse was estimated at around a hundred and fifty million pounds or more.
A report by two committees of MPs didn't hold back. It described Carillion's collapse in four words.
The auditors were criticised too. The MPs accused the auditor KPMG of signing off what they called increasingly fantastical figures. KPMG was later fined by the regulator over its work.

vis.text: The auditor signed it all off.

beats.say: Part seven. The lessons.
Carillion's story is a warning about chasing growth at any cost, and about governments relying too heavily on a few giant contractors.

vis.title: Lessons from Carillion
items: Winning work too cheaply is a trap
Dividends paid from debt are a warning

beats.say: A company can look enormous, important and permanent. But if the cash doesn't add up, size won't save it. It just means more people get hurt when it falls.

vis.text: Size won't save you if the cash doesn't add up.
